title: AI in the Classroom: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Multilingual Learners in Secondary Education
venue: ASRC Procedia: Global Perspectives in Science and Scholarship
extended_summary:
This paper asks how intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) can support multilingual learners in secondary education, with particular attention to which system components and design features are associated with better learning outcomes. The review focuses on the challenge that multilingual students must learn academic content while also developing proficiency in the language of instruction, and it frames ITS as a possible tool for delivering personalized, language-sensitive support.

The paper synthesizes 110 peer-reviewed studies on ITS design, implementation, and effectiveness. It examines core components such as learner modeling, domain knowledge, pedagogical strategy engines, and user interface design, along with features including Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, Performance Factor Analysis, natural language processing, speech recognition, automated writing feedback, multimodal instruction, affect detection, and culturally responsive content. The population is multilingual learners in secondary education, with examples and discussion oriented toward classroom use in linguistically diverse secondary settings.

The review concludes that ITS can improve comprehension, retention, confidence, and engagement when they provide adaptive personalization, multimodal support, and linguistically sensitive feedback. It also argues that culturally relevant content, inclusive interface design, teacher training, infrastructure readiness, and ethical data governance are important for successful implementation. The paper notes that generative AI may expand personalization and interaction, but it also raises concerns about bias, privacy, and cultural preservation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it does not present a new controlled study or meta-analytic synthesis with pooled estimates in the text provided. The evidence is therefore informative but primarily narrative and secondary, making it closer to a qualitative/correlational review than high-credibility causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for multilingual secondary learners, especially for literacy, science comprehension, and engagement, but it does not quantify effects. Because the reported impact is promising yet unmeasured and heterogeneous across studies, the overall impact tier is modest/unclear rather than strong.

interventions.use_case: systematic review of ITS for multilingual learners in secondary education, emphasizing learner modeling, adaptive feedback, multimodal delivery, and culturally responsive scaffolding

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ITS with linguistically sensitive feedback, multimodal support, and bilingual scaffolding were associated with improved reading comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, and confidence in academic writing for multilingual secondary learners. It cites a European pilot of FeedBook and other studies as showing measurable gains, but no pooled effect size or exact n is reported in the paper text.
finding.measure: reading comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, academic writing confidence
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that in mathematics and science, multilingual students performed better when ITS provided bilingual glossaries, visual scaffolding, and step-by-step explanations. This is presented as convergent evidence from the reviewed literature rather than a single controlled estimate, so no effect size or exact sample size is available in the text.
finding.measure: subject-matter assessment performance in mathematics and science
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly reports positive effects on learner confidence and engagement when ITS used adaptive personalization, supportive feedback, and multimodal interaction. These outcomes are described as improved through reduced frustration and more inclusive interaction design, but the article does not provide pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals.
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that ITS supported comprehension, retention, and learner self-reflection through techniques such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, performance factor analysis, spaced repetition, and metacognitive prompts. This is a narrative synthesis of the reviewed literature, so the text does not report a pooled effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation.
finding.measure: retention, metacognitive reflection, self-monitoring of learning
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that implementation success depends on teacher training, infrastructure readiness, ethical data governance, and careful bias/ privacy protections. These are framed as enabling conditions and risks rather than measured outcomes, so there is no quantitative effect size; the overall message is that institutional impact can be positive if implementation supports are in place, but harmful if bias and privacy issues are ignored.
finding.measure: implementation readiness, teacher training, infrastructure, ethical governance
